Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight

Ju Dong1,†, Xinyu Xiao4, Yiming Zhou4,†, Tianshuo Yang2, Xuerong Liu2,
Lei Zhang1, Jian Chen5, Haocheng Zhao3, Yu Fu1, Yujie Wei4, Diwen Zheng3,
Alois Christian Knoll3, Angela P. Schoellig3, Ping Luo2,∗, Jianwei Zhang1 ††thanks: $ˆ†$Project leads. $ˆ*$Corresponding author. Affiliation: TAMS (Technical Aspects of Multimodal Systems), Department of Informatics, University of Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany. Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China. Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Germany. Affiliation: Kinetix AI, China. Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China.
Abstract

Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world–action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion–hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Ψ0\Psi_{0} and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/.

I Introduction

Everyday humanoid tasks require coordinated actions over time. To place a basket on a table, the robot must raise and position the basket while maintaining its grasp until the table supports it. To load a washer, it must open the door, carry a T-shirt to the drum without dropping it, and release it only once it is inside. These tasks connect whole-body motion with hand interaction: an execution decision concerns both the scene a command sequence will reach and the relationships among commands along the way.

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate commands from images and language instructions [1, 2, 3], while humanoid models incorporate human motion and predictive representations [4, 5, 6, 7]. When an action generator proposes several sequences, the robot must decide which one to execute. Latent world models provide predictions for goal-directed planning [8, 9]. Most world–action models use future prediction to improve command generation [10, 11, 12] rather than to compare sampled sequences before execution. Existing verifiers use VLM judgments [13, 14], while DreamTrajectory combines predicted trajectory agreement with action smoothness [15]. Two signals are relevant for evaluating proposed humanoid actions: predicted visual progress evaluates the endpoint relative to a task goal, while temporal consistency evaluates relationships among commands within the sequence.

We introduce action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world–action model (WAM) that uses both signals for humanoid loco-manipulation (Fig. 1). An action generator proposes joint motion–hand command sequences; an action-conditioned endpoint predictor scores their visual progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, and a joint temporal prior scores their temporal consistency. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose action-conditioned latent foresight, which scores generated motion–hand sequences before execution using predicted visual progress and a learned joint temporal prior.

  • •

    We develop action consistency regularization for latent prediction. A training-only inverse action decoder reconstructs the first demonstrated command from both observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predicted features to retain information about the executed action.

  • •

    We evaluate ten SIMPLE [16] simulation tasks and seven real-robot tasks, including unseen object configurations. Our method exceeds the evaluated baselines in average success; closed-loop ablations show gains from action consistency regularization and joint temporal scoring.

II Related Work

II-A Humanoid VLAs and World–Action Models

VLA policies transfer vision–language representations to command generation [1, 2]. Heterogeneous co-training improves open-world generalization [3], and diffusion action heads generate continuous action chunks [17]. For humanoids, EgoVLA uses retargeted wrist and hand motion [18], Ψ0\Psi_{0} exploits egocentric pretraining [4], and WholeBodyVLA learns manipulation and locomotion latent actions from video before decoding upper-body and locomotion commands [5].

World–action models couple prediction with command generation. DreamZero jointly models video and actions [10]; DiT4DiT and MotionWAM condition action or motion diffusion on intermediate video-model features [11, 6]. MotionWAM combines SONIC motion codes with hand-control channels [6], while ω\omega-0 generates controller-compatible actions from future embeddings [7]. WholeBodyWAM pretrains a motion expert to learn whole-body motion priors for robot action generation [19]. Fast-WAM and InternW0-Δ\Delta use future supervision during training without generating video at test time [12, 20]. In our method, the action generator supplies command sequences, and each sequence prefix is scored before execution using action-conditioned prediction and temporal consistency.

II-B Action Supervision for Latent Prediction

Latent world models predict action-conditioned feature transitions for goal-directed planning [8, 9]. V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense video features [21], and a study of JEPA world models examines how representation, predictor, and planner choices affect physical planning [22]. VLA-JEPA learns VLM latent tokens through future-state prediction and uses them to condition flow-matching action generation [23]. Related models combine feature prediction with action modeling [24], or predict future latent states alongside actions [25]. Our predictor takes the proposed command prefix as input and estimates its endpoint features, allowing command sequences sampled from the same observation to receive different visual scores.

Action supervision can also arise from discrete or constrained continuous latents [26, 27], inverse dynamics that turn generated video into executable actions [28], or visual correspondences [29]. Our action consistency regularization uses an inverse action decoder to reconstruct the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, providing a training objective for the endpoint predictor rather than a test-time action decoder.

II-C Temporal Action Priors and Sequence Scoring

Action-sequence models [30, 31] and cross-embodiment action priors [32] learn regularities that guide generation. PRISM combines state-conditioned priors with planning distributions [33], and DynaGuide uses learned dynamics to steer diffusion [34]. Action verification evaluates proposed actions before execution: RoboMonkey learns action preferences with a VLM verifier [13], while FOREWARN aligns predicted latent rollouts with behavior descriptions for VLM-based action choice [14].

DreamTrajectory combines agreement with intended end-effector trajectories and fixed smoothness penalties [15]; LeWAM’s DemoDPO uses demonstration preferences for offline policy refinement [25]. Our temporal prior learns to predict the next complete command from the initial robot state and preceding motion–hand commands. Its prediction error is combined with visual progress when scoring proposed actions.

III Method

III-A Problem Formulation and Receding-Horizon Scoring

Given an egocentric image oto_{t}, instruction ℓ\ell, and proprioceptive state sts_{t}, our action generator samples NN normalized command chunks At(i)∈ℝH×daA_{t}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}:

Vi\displaystyle V_{i} =dist⁡(zt,zg)−dist⁡(z^(i),zg),\displaystyle=\operatorname{dist}(z_{t},z_{g})-\operatorname{dist}(\hat{z}^{(i)},z_{g}),

III-B Action Generation

Qwen3-VL-2B [36] encodes the image and instruction into separate policy tokens ctactc_{t}^{\mathrm{act}} and prediction tokens ctc_{t} (Fig. 2). Action DiT [37] alternates cross-attention to ctactc_{t}^{\mathrm{act}} with self-attention over state tokens, learned tokens, and noisy action tokens. Its flow-matching velocity head [38] generates command sequences through numerical integration from initial noise ξ\xi.

III-C Action-Conditioned Endpoint Dynamics

We fine-tune the V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L/16 encoder (384 px) [21] with its official self-supervised training recipe on HIW-500 [39], over 500 hours of whole-body humanoid demonstrations collected through Unitree G1 teleoperation in real homes. We then freeze the resulting encoder for task training and inference; it also extracts the demonstration subgoals. Let Φ\Phi denote this encoder applied to a single image, repeated to the encoder clip length, with its last temporal feature block retained. Current, goal, and future images are encoded separately:

𝐟t=Φ⁡(ot),𝐟g=Φ⁡(gt),𝐟t+h=Φ⁡(ot+h).\mathbf{f}_{t}=\Phi(o_{t}),\quad\mathbf{f}_{g}=\Phi(g_{t}),\quad\mathbf{f}_{t+h}=\Phi(o_{t+h}). (3)

Thus zt=pool⁡(𝐟t)z_{t}=\operatorname{pool}(\mathbf{f}_{t}) and zg=pool⁡(𝐟g)z_{g}=\operatorname{pool}(\mathbf{f}_{g}). During training, the demonstrated prefix Bt=(at,0,…,at,h−1)B_{t}=(a_{t,0},\ldots,a_{t,h-1}) starting at time tt is paired with the observation ot+ho_{t+h}.

A command encoder CηC_{\eta} produces one token per command with positional encoding. We add the mean of the prediction tokens, c¯t\bar{c}_{t}, to each command token, giving qt​(B)=Cη​(B)+c¯tq_{t}(B)=C_{\eta}(B)+\bar{c}_{t}. The endpoint predictor is

𝐟^t+h=𝒫θ​(𝐟t,qt​(Bt)).\widehat{\mathbf{f}}_{t+h}=\mathcal{P}_{\theta}(\mathbf{f}_{t},q_{t}(B_{t})). (4)

All trainable components are optimized jointly with this objective.

IV Experiments

IV-A Experimental Setup

Tasks and demonstrations: We evaluate ten tasks from SIMPLE [16], a simulation benchmark for humanoid loco-manipulation (Fig. 3), using its official demonstrations collected through motion planning and VR teleoperation. Its standard 36-dimensional interface contains 14 hand joint targets and 22 channels for arm, torso, and locomotion control. We run ten trials per task at each of three randomization levels: L0 varies distractors and backgrounds; L1 adds materials and lighting; L2 adds initial object and robot poses. Real-robot evaluation covers seven G1 tasks (Figs. 1 and 3) under standard conditions and unseen object configurations, with ten trials per task and condition. The real-robot interface combines a 64-dimensional SONIC motion latent with 14 hand joint targets. Demonstrations are collected using SONIC: 400 per task, except for 200 in Place Basket on Table. Unseen configurations change object identity, placement, orientation, or appearance to states absent from the corresponding task demonstrations, while preserving the task objective.

Visual subgoals: For offline subgoal extraction, we mean-pool all spatiotemporal tokens from each repeated-image clip using the frozen visual encoder, accumulate feature changes between consecutive frames, and sample JJ subgoal images at evenly spaced values of this cumulative change. The images remain in temporal order, and standard and unseen-configuration trials use the same sequence for each task; the baselines do not use subgoals.

Implementation: Table I summarizes the platforms and implementation settings. Each method trained in our experiments uses a separate policy per task. Simulation policies use 40,000 training steps and a per-GPU batch size of 32; real-robot policies use 90,000 steps and a per-GPU batch size of 4.

Baselines: For the simulation comparison, we train and evaluate DiT4DiT [11], Fast-WAM [12], and VLA-JEPA [23]; task-success results for the other baselines are taken from SIMPLE [16]. For the real-robot comparison, we train and evaluate GR00T N1.7 [17], Ψ0\Psi_{0} [4], and DiT4DiT.

IV-B Task Performance

Tables II–IV report closed-loop task success.

Simulation: Our method achieves 89.7% average success across ten SIMPLE tasks, compared with 82.0% for DiT4DiT, 73.7% for Ψ0\Psi_{0}, and 49.0% for VLA-JEPA. Success averages 95.6% on the six main tasks and 80.8% on the four additional tasks. OpenFaucet is the most difficult task, with 17/30 successes.

Real robot: Our method achieves 85.7% success under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, compared with 70.0% and 48.6% for GR00T N1.7, the strongest baseline. Under standard conditions, our method succeeds in all ten trials on four tasks. The gain of 15.7 percentage points comes mainly from Load Washer (10/10 versus 2/10). GR00T N1.7 failures on this task include dropping the T-shirt during transport, releasing it before it is inside the drum, and not opening the washer door. The first two resemble the Place Basket on Table failure in Fig. 1, where the basket falls during placement: the grasp is not maintained until the object reaches its target. Dispose of Trash is the only task where our method has a lower success rate than GR00T N1.7; its failures include the partial lid opening in Fig. 6. Under unseen configurations, baseline success ranges from 0/10 to 6/10 per task. Our method has the highest or tied-highest success on all seven tasks and reaches at least 7/10 on four of them.

IV-C Qualitative Results and Generalization

In Water Plant and Load Washer (Fig. 4), the robot uses its right hand in standard trials and its left hand in the unseen object configurations with a reversed watering-can spout or a T-shirt placed on its left, completing both tasks. The left-hand T-shirt grasp does not appear in the demonstrations.

IV-D Data Efficiency

We compare training with 25, 50, and 100 demonstrations per task on five SIMPLE tasks: OpenOven, PickAndPlaceAndHugContainer, OpenFaucet, OpenTrashCan, and Mobile P&P.

At each of the three demonstration budgets, our method has higher average success than Ψ0\Psi_{0} on this five-task subset (Fig. 5). With 100 demonstrations per task, it reaches 84.0%, compared with 56.7% for Ψ0\Psi_{0}, a gain of 27.3 percentage points.

IV-E Failure Analysis

OpenFaucet accounts for 13 of 31 simulation failures (41.9%). The robot repeatedly moves its hand near the faucet handle but fails to open it (Fig. 6(a)). In Dispose of Trash, pressing the pedal opens the lid only partly; the robot keeps holding the object and does not release it (Fig. 6(b)). In Collect Toy with Cart, the robot lifts the soft toy but cannot hold it securely, and the toy falls before reaching the cart (Fig. 6(c)).

IV-F Ablation Studies

We evaluate three design choices through closed-loop task success: prediction formulation, action consistency regularization, and temporal scoring.

IV-F1 Prediction Formulation

The feature-shift variant jointly encodes a short clip and predicts each visual feature block from the preceding ones. Command tokens are resampled to one group per visual block, added position-wise to the VLM prediction tokens, and interleaved with the blocks in a block-causal predictor; at inference, the current image is repeated to form the clip, and the predicted blocks are pooled for scoring. The endpoint model instead encodes current and future observations separately and predicts a single endpoint from the first hh commands. With joint encoding, feature-shift inputs can carry information from later frames during training that the repeated-image clip lacks at inference; separate encoding avoids this mismatch. The endpoint model reaches 89.7% versus 84.3% on the ten SIMPLE tasks (Table V), improving both task sets.

Component ablations: Both ablations use the four additional SIMPLE tasks in Table III, on which the full model has lower average success than on the six main tasks: ten complete episodes per task at each level (L0/L1/L2), totaling 120 per configuration. Within each ablation, configurations share demonstration data, training budgets, test initial conditions, and subgoals.

IV-F2 Action Consistency Regularization

We train two models with action consistency regularization enabled or disabled, keeping the other objectives unchanged. Both use visual-only scoring at inference (Table VI).

Action consistency regularization increases success from 66/120 episodes (55.0%) to 79/120 (65.8%), a gain of 10.8 percentage points. Success is higher on all four tasks.

IV-F3 Temporal Prior

We use the trained action generator, endpoint predictor, and joint prior from the full model, and compare alternative temporal scores at every decision (Table VII). The first- and second-order penalties average ‖ak−ak−1‖22/da\|a_{k}-a_{k-1}\|_{2}^{2}/d_{a} and ‖ak−2​ak−1+ak−2‖22/da\|a_{k}-2a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\|_{2}^{2}/d_{a}, respectively, over valid steps of the normalized command prefix. The factorized prior predicts each group from its own history and the current state; the joint prior uses the histories of both groups.

The factorized prior is trained with the other components frozen, using the joint prior’s group weights and a parameter count within 1%. All temporal scores use a fixed β=0.1\beta=0.1; visual-only scoring sets β=0\beta=0.

The joint prior achieves the highest closed-loop success among the tested scoring methods: 97/120 episodes (80.8%). This is 15.0 percentage points above visual-only scoring and 9.2 above the factorized prior. Scoring with first- and second-order smoothness penalties achieves 67.5% and 70.0% success, respectively, 1.7–4.2 percentage points above visual-only scoring, compared with 5.8 for the factorized prior. The joint prior also exceeds the factorized prior on each of the four tasks, consistent with scoring dependencies between motion and hand commands.

IV-G Inference Cost and Deployment

Our method uses less than half the GPU memory of DiT4DiT and Fast-WAM and runs faster (Table VIII); GR00T N1.6 remains faster at similar memory use. Our task-success evaluations use the RTX 4090D listed in Table I. In an additional onboard deployment test, our method runs on the robot’s Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), averaging 12.84 GB of system memory and an inference frequency of 0.73 Hz across seven tasks.

V Conclusion and Future Work

Action-conditioned latent foresight scores generated motion–hand sequences by predicted visual progress and temporal consistency before execution. It achieves 89.7% success in simulation and 85.7% and 65.7% on the real robot under standard and unseen object configurations. In closed-loop ablations, action consistency regularization adds 10.8 percentage points and the joint prior exceeds the factorized prior by 9.2 percentage points.

The failure cases include incomplete opening of articulated mechanisms and loss of grasp on a soft object. The visual score also relies on task-specific demonstration subgoal images. In the onboard deployment test, inference runs at 0.73 Hz. Future work will add contact and object-state supervision to latent prediction and extend temporal scoring across consecutive command chunks.
